summary: Kole Jain tears down a viewer's restaurant management software website that is clean and functional but feels soulless, then redesigns it from visual identity through layout to animation. His diagnosis is that the site says it is for restaurant owners but never looks like it has heard of a restaurant: it has no images at all, which he reads as a sign of vibe coding. He builds a visual identity from a single moody image, pulls an earthy palette and accents from it, swaps a monospace font for a serif paired with the existing sans, and adds feature icons. He then 'Frankensteins' a wireframe from sections of other sites and fills each section with the same repeatable recipe of background, noise texture, type and scattered images. Finally, he gives the site an animation identity of motion themes that repeat, that direct the eye, and that soften hard breaks between sections. For a design system, the lesson is to define layout and visual identity carefully so different identities can be swapped into the same layout, and to choose imagery, type and motion for the feeling that fits the brand and its audience rather than from a formula.
key_ideas: A site can be clean, compact and well animated yet still feel soulless if it does not relate to the people it is for.
A website with no images anywhere feels robotic; he calls it a telltale sign the site was vibe coded.
A strong site relates to its audience visually (laptops and keyboards for freelancers) and has one actionable heading that promises what the product does.
Start the visual identity from one moody image instead of bright, sterile light modes or flat, typical dark modes.
Pull the base palette from the tones in the mood images, then add a few accent colors.
Pairing a serif with the existing sans adds personality (like a printed menu); the monospace font did not fit.
The identity should come from what conveys the feeling for the brand, not from a formula.
'Frankensteining' means picking sections from other sites to work out the message and page flow, then keeping only the wireframe.
Once the wireframe and identity exist, building each section becomes almost formulaic: background, texture, text, images.
Things that look scattered and random are actually ordered: larger elements below, smaller on top, with a safe margin around text.
Because the layout and the visual identity were both carefully defined, different identities can be swapped into the same layout for very different feelings.
Animation is usually an afterthought, but repeated motion themes can form an animation identity for the brand.
Motion should direct the eye to the focal point and smooth hard breaks between sections.
When several images all matter, rotating them on a timer encourages people to see every one.

topics.name: Landing pages
topics.summary: A full teardown and rebuild of a SaaS landing page: hero, logo ribbon, how-it-works, feature tabs, testimonials, CTA and footer, assembled from references and given a consistent identity.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: His workflow runs from diagnosis to a visual identity deck, then a Frankensteined wireframe, then section-by-section visuals, then animation.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: The palette is pulled from the earthy tones of moody images, with a few accent colors taken from another site (Anchor, as heard); section backgrounds use brand colors, images or cream.

topics.name: Typography
topics.summary: Keep the existing sans, replace a monospace that did not fit with a serif for personality, and split hero heading lines between them.

topics.name: Icons and imagery
topics.summary: Images that relate to the audience are what make the site feel built for restaurants; feature icons are drawn in the accent colors; scattered image assets follow a hidden order.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Hero buttons sit at least twice the heading-to-subtext distance below the subtext, and scattered images keep a safe margin around the text.

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Darkened edges pull attention to the center of the hero, and motion is used to direct the eye to the focal point.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: Animation should be part of the brand: repeated motion themes, eye-directing motion, and slide-and-blur transitions that remove hard breaks between sections.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Feature images rotate on a timer and zoom in slightly on hover.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: A good-by-most-standards site can still feel soulless; the fix is conveying a feeling that fits the brand, not following a formula or making it look more modern.

topics.name: AI-assisted design
topics.summary: He links an image-less, robotic site to vibe coding and argues that feeling and identity are what vibe coding cannot supply (from the title) [inferred]; the sponsor pitches an MCP for prototyping wireframes.

rules.rule: Show images that relate to the target audience on a product site; do not ship a site with no images at all.
rules.why: A site with no images anywhere feels robotic, and the source calls it a telltale sign of vibe coding; images are how the site relates to its users and builds trust.
rules.evidence: no images anywhere

rules.rule: Use a single, actionable hero heading that promises exactly what the software does.
rules.why: It is one of the things that makes Actual relate to its users and build trust.
rules.evidence: a single, very actionable heading

rules.rule: Start the visual identity from one moody image: crop it, darken it, add noise and put the brand name on it, instead of starting from a bright light mode or a flat dark mode; then gather more images with the same moody vibe.
rules.why: It gets away from bright, sterile light modes and flat, typical dark modes, and the site's feeling starts from the visual identity.
rules.evidence: start with a single image that's more moody

rules.rule: Pull the base color palette from the tones in the brand's mood images, then add a few accent colors.
rules.why: It keeps the palette tied to the feeling of the images; accents give extra colors to play with.
rules.evidence: pulling out some of those earthy tones from the images themselves

rules.rule: Pair a serif with the sans to add personality when the brand calls for it, instead of a monospace that does not fit.
rules.why: The serif adds personality, like a printed menu for a restaurant brand; the monospace was not working.
rules.evidence: mix in a serif font to add a little more personality

rules.rule: Draw feature icons in the brand's accent colors so each icon stands for one main feature of the product.
rules.why: The icons come to represent the main features of the product, and the same icons from the brand deck are reused in the features section.
rules.evidence: Using our accents, I'm going to add in a few icons

rules.rule: Do not derive the visual identity from a formula; choose each element for the feeling it conveys and whether it makes sense for the brand.
rules.why: It is all about what conveys the feeling and makes sense for the brand; he calls this one of the most important things about building the identity.
rules.evidence: none of this came from a formula

rules.rule: Work out the page's message and flow by assembling a wireframe from sections of reference sites, then keep only the wireframe and discard their visuals.
rules.why: It creates a site flow that resonates, while the look comes from your own identity.
rules.evidence: Frankensteining a site to work out our message and site flow

rules.rule: Add extra social proof, such as testimonials, beyond a logo ribbon.
rules.why: Logos are nice, but it is typically good to have a little extra social proof.
rules.evidence: typically it's good to have a little extra social proof

rules.rule: In feature sections, make the images bigger and cut most of the text.
rules.why: He borrows Miro's full-screen color tabs but wants the images to dominate the page.
rules.evidence: cut like 90% of this text

rules.rule: Add subtle noise to image or color backgrounds behind text.
rules.why: It adds texture and also helps the contrast of the text.
rules.evidence: a little bit of noise, which will also help with contrast for the text

rules.rule: Place hero buttons below the subtext at a gap at least twice the gap between the heading and the subtext.
rules.why: The large heading already has a good amount of distance between the baseline where the letters sit and the actual bottom of the heading.
values: at least twice the distance of the heading and subtext
rules.evidence: at least twice the distance of the heading and subtext

rules.rule: When scattering image assets around text, put larger elements below and smaller elements on top, and always keep a safe margin around the text.
rules.why: Things should feel scattered and random while actually being ordered.
rules.evidence: larger elements below, smaller elements on top

rules.rule: Darken the edges of the hero to draw attention to the center.
rules.why: It really draws attention to the center where the text sits.
rules.evidence: darken the edges

rules.rule: Match each section's background and texture to the feeling it needs, for example a cream background with no noise and a graph-paper texture for a clean software feel.
rules.why: It lets a section lean into the clean software feel while staying in the identity.
rules.evidence: a cream background with no noise

rules.rule: Define a few motion themes and repeat them throughout the site, instead of one-off effects.
rules.why: Themes that repeat, rather than happening once, form the basis of an animation visual identity and make motion feel part of the brand.
rules.evidence: they don't just happen once, but are repeated throughout the website

rules.rule: Use motion to direct the eye to each section's focal point; on the hero, the focal point is the text.
rules.why: When applying motion to any design, the aim is to direct the eye and the focal point.
rules.evidence: directing the eye and the focal point

rules.rule: Soften a hard break between the hero and the next section: slide the hero elements off screen and blur the text while the new section slides over the top; apply the same idea in reverse on the CTA section.
rules.why: It makes the hero feel like part of the background and the change smoother than a hard break.
rules.evidence: slide the elements off the screen and blur our text

rules.rule: When several feature images all matter, rotate them automatically on a timer and add a slight zoom on hover.
rules.why: It encourages the user to check them all out and brings a dry middle section to life.
rules.evidence: have them on a timer rotating automatically

rules.rule: Add texture images to the identity that fit the darker colors and the audience, for example a counter with pots and pans and measuring spoons, or a tablet to stay closer to the software theme.
rules.why: With the darker colors he wants some texture in the identity.
rules.evidence: With these darker colors, I want to get a bit of texture in here

rules.rule: In a how-it-works section, make it less step-like and use much bigger background images that show who would use the product, with stronger noise and mid-size text.
rules.why: The section should talk about how the product works while the background images reinforce who would use it.
rules.evidence: really use those background images to reinforce who would use our product

rules.rule: Define the layout (wireframe) and the visual identity carefully and separately, so a different identity can be swapped into the same layout.
rules.why: Because both were defined with care, swapping identities into the same layout gives wildly different feelings; he calls this how you really master building engaging landing pages.
rules.evidence: swap out different identities into the same layout

decisions.question: Where should the look of the site start?

options.name: Bright light mode
options.when: Not recommended here; he wants to get away from it.

options.name: Typical dark mode
options.when: Not recommended here; he wants to get away from it.

options.name: One moody image
options.effect: A cropped, darkened image with noise and the brand name sets a feeling that the palette, textures and fonts then follow.
options.when: When the site needs to feel like it belongs to its audience and stand out.

decisions.recommendation: Start from a single moody image, because it escapes the sterile light and flat dark defaults and sets the feeling first.
decisions.evidence: To get away from the bright and sterile light modes and the flat and typical dark modes

decisions.question: Should the site show images, and what kind?

options.name: No images
options.effect: Clean and compact but robotic; the source calls it a telltale sign of vibe coding.

options.name: Images that relate to the audience
options.effect: Restaurant items, kitchen counters and tablets (or laptops and keyboards for freelancers) make the site feel built for its users and build trust.
options.when: Whenever the site says who it is for.

decisions.recommendation: Use images that relate to the audience, because that is how the site relates to users and builds trust.

decisions.question: Use one type style or pair a serif with the sans?

options.name: All sans-serif
options.when: When the brand does not need extra personality [inferred].

options.name: Sans with a monospace
options.effect: The original site's choice; he says it was not working.

options.name: Sans paired with a serif
options.effect: Adds personality, like a printed menu; hero heading lines can be split between the two.
options.when: When the brand has a character the serif can echo, such as restaurants.

decisions.recommendation: Keep the sans and mix in a serif for personality.
decisions.evidence: mix in a serif font to add a little more personality

decisions.question: What background should each section use?

options.name: A main brand color with a little noise
options.effect: Textured color that also helps text contrast.
options.when: Hero, drawing on the brand deck.

options.name: Images with stronger noise
options.effect: Moody, audience-specific background with mid-size text that reinforces who uses the product.
options.when: Sections about how the product works.

options.name: Cream with no noise and a graph-paper texture
options.effect: A cleaner software feel while keeping the identity.

decisions.recommendation: Vary it per section from the brand deck, matching each section's purpose.
decisions.evidence: From the brand, we can have these main colors to work with or an image

decisions.question: How should the page move between the hero and the next section on scroll?

options.name: Hard break
options.effect: A pretty hard break between the upper and lower sections.

options.name: Slide off and blur, with the next section sliding over
options.effect: The hero feels like part of the background and the change is smooth.
options.when: At the hero, and in reverse at the CTA, the page's bookends.

decisions.recommendation: Slide the hero elements off and blur the text while the new section slides over the top.
decisions.evidence: we have a pretty hard break between the upper and the lower sections

decisions.question: How should a set of important feature images be shown?

options.name: Static
options.effect: The middle of the page feels a little dry.
options.when: Not recommended when every image matters.

options.name: Auto-rotating on a timer, with a slight zoom on hover
options.effect: Encourages users to see every image and brings the section to life.
options.when: When each image is important and you want users to check them all out.

decisions.recommendation: Rotate them automatically on a timer and add a slight zoom on hover.
decisions.evidence: each of these four images is quite important

process.detail: Compare the site with sites that clearly relate to their audience and find the gap, for example saying who it is for but never showing it.

process.step: Set the mood with one image
process.detail: Pick one moody image, crop it, darken it, layer on noise and add the brand name; then gather more images with the same vibe.
Pull earthy tones from the images for a simple palette and take a few accent colors from another site (Anchor, as heard).
Add textures that fit the darker colors, such as a counter with pots and pans or, closer to software, a tablet.
Keep what works (the sans), replace what doesn't (the monospace) and mix in a serif for personality.

process.step: Make feature icons and finish the deck
process.detail: Draw icons in the accent colors for the main features, then add more images and the logo mark.
Choose a reference for each section (hero, logo ribbon, how it works, features, testimonials, CTA, footer), note what to change, then keep only the wireframe.

process.step: Build each section with the same recipe
process.detail: Background (brand color or image), texture (noise level), text (serif and sans split, subtext, buttons with the right spacing), image assets in a hidden order, then darkened edges.
Apply the same recipe to each wireframe section, varying background and texture to fit its purpose.
Define repeated motion themes, direct the eye to focal points, smooth hard section breaks, and bring dry sections to life with rotation and hover zoom.

caveats: Sponsor segment for Relume: its MCP, '1,000+ components', paid plans and a '7-day free trial' are a product plug, not design guidance.
Self-promotion: a link to submit sites for future videos and Figma assets in the description.
Calling an image-less site a 'telltale sign' of vibe coding is the presenter's opinion.
Most of the result is shown on screen; the transcript gives no exact colors, font names, noise amounts, durations or easing values.
Auto-caption names: 'Atios' is read as Attio; 'Anchor' (the accent color site), 'Actual', 'Superpowered' and 'Amigo AI' are spelled as heard and not verified.
One teardown of one restaurant SaaS site; the serif and moody-image choices fit that brand and are not presented as universal.
